newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN General Assembly expected to end nuke test era.
newsitem.headline: UN General Assembly expected to end nuke test era.

text.p: Australia and more than 100 countries on Monday afternoon seek U.N. General Assembly approval of the nuclear test ban treaty through a legal manoeuvre aimed at circumventing India's veto.

After three years of negotiations, the 61-nation Geneva -based Conference on Disarmament was unable to open the treaty for signature because India refused to give its consent. Under that conference's rules, decisions must be by consensus.

In contrast, the General Assembly can vote by a two-thirds or a majority vote to approve the treaty. In either case diplomats believe the sponsors of the resolution, numbering about 120, can easily muster the needed votes among the 160 or so states expected to attend the session.
Diplomats said that Pakistan as well as Israel, which has long been secretive about its own nuclear programme, are among the sponsors of the document.

Debate on a resolution, drawn up by Australia, is expected to be short and a vote could come as early as Tuesday. The resolution would have the assembly adopt the treaty and request U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali to open it up for signature.

The treaty, known as the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, or CTBT, however, does not come into force until 44 states with a nuclear potential sign it. This includes India, which exploded a device in 1974.
But most diplomats believe that once a country signs the treaty, it must abide by it even if the treaty is not legally in force.

India since the mid-1960s has argued that the nuclear powers needed a timetable to eliminate their existing arsenals before it gives up its own option. It also opposes the treaty's call for a review conference in three years to consider further steps if the treaty has not gone into force.

India's U.N. ambassador, Prakash Shah, last week gave notice that his country would block the treaty from coming into force by refusing to sign it. "The question of being isolated does not bother us at all. We will not sign it."
His colleague from Geneva, Arundhati Ghose, said that he found it "disingenous, at best, to say that five countries need nuclear weapons for their security and nobdoy else does."

Australia's Richard Butler, who sought to bypass India's veto by bringing the treaty to assembly, said that a prohibition on testing by so-called undeclared states "would mightily affect whatever plans they might have to develop the quantity and quality of nuclear weapons."
"And that's part of what is being sought here."

Since the United States exploded the world's first atomic bomb in on July 16, 1945 in the New Mexico desert there have been 2,045 known nuclear tests, 1,030 of them American, followed by the 715 in the former Soviet Union. The other three known nuclear powers are France, Britain and China.

"It will be a victory for the people," said Dan Plesch, director of the British-American Security Information Council, an independent arms control research group. He contends that polls show strong public support in industrial states, from 61 to 85 percent, including in the United States.

The future of the treaty also depends on a quick signature from President Bill Clinton when he is expected to visit the United Nations later this month. Should he lose the November elections, the Republican Party platform says the United States needs "development of nuclear weapons and their periodic testing" for its security interest.
